title: Floating and sinking: why a steel ship floats and a pebble sinks

summary.text: A loaded steel ship can weigh tens of thousands of tonnes and still float, while a pebble that fits in your hand sinks at once. A ball of kitchen foil sinks, but the same foil folded into a small boat floats and carries coins. Your child tests why, with foil boats, a potato in salty water and a bottle that dives. They learn what density is, why a hollow shape floats, and why salty water holds things up better than fresh water. They also learn why ice floats, how submarines and fish rise and sink, and how a pattern like 'heavy things sink' is tested before anyone trusts it.
summary.art: A bucket of water on a kitchen floor with a foil ball sunk at the bottom and a small foil boat on the surface carrying a few coins.

intro.hook: Drop a ball of kitchen foil into a bucket of water. It sinks. Now squeeze the same piece of foil into a little boat and set it on the water. It floats. It is the same foil, with the same weight. What changed?
intro.text: Nothing was added and nothing was taken away. Only the shape changed. A boat shape holds a big pocket of air, and the pocket pushes aside a lot of water. In this unit you find out how much water a thing must push aside to float. You test foil boats with coins, you float a potato in salty water, and you make a bottle diver that sinks and rises when you squeeze it.
intro.art: Two photographs side by side: a crumpled foil ball sunk in a bucket of water, and an open foil boat floating on the same water.

outcomes: I can explain that a thing floats when it is lighter than the same amount of water, which scientists call less dense.
I can explain why a hollow shape such as a boat floats, even when it is made of a material that sinks.
I can run a fair test that changes one thing at a time, count the results, and show them in a table or a bar chart.
I can explain why the same thing can sink in fresh water and float in salty water.
I can explain why ice and oil float on water, and why liquids can sit in layers.
I can explain how submarines, fish and balloons rise and sink by changing how dense they are.
I can say why a pattern such as 'heavy things sink' must be tested before it is trusted.

explanations.concept: What makes a thing float: lighter than the water it pushes aside
explanations.definition: A thing floats when it is lighter than the same amount of water it pushes aside. A thing sinks when it is heavier than that water.
explanations.description: When you put something into water, it pushes some water out of the way. Imagine a bucket of water the same size as the part of the thing that is under the surface. If that water weighs more than the whole thing, the water wins, and the thing floats. If the water weighs less, the thing wins, and it sinks. This is why size and weight alone do not settle it. A big ship is heavy, but it is also very big, and it pushes aside a huge amount of water. A pebble is light, but it is small and solid, so it pushes aside only a little water. What matters is how heavy a thing is for its size.
examples: A cork floats because a piece of cork is lighter than the same amount of water.
A steel spoon sinks because steel is much heavier than the same amount of water.
A big ship floats because the water it pushes aside weighs as much as the ship.
explanations.art: A foil boat in water, with a dotted bucket-shaped outline of the water it pushes aside and a label that says this water weighs as much as the boat.

explanations.concept: Density: how much stuff is packed into a space
explanations.definition: Density tells you how much mass there is in a certain volume. Something dense is heavy for its size.
explanations.description: A litre of water has a mass of 1 kilogram. So one millilitre of water has a mass of 1 gram. Scientists use water as the measuring stick. A material that is denser than water, such as iron, sinks in it. Iron is almost 8 times denser than water. A material that is less dense than water, such as most woods, floats. Cooking oil is a little less dense than water, and ice is a little less dense than liquid water. Some very hard woods, such as ebony, are denser than water and sink. The word density comes from the idea of how closely stuff is packed together.
examples: Aluminium is denser than water, but only about 2.7 times, so a thin aluminium foil is easily shaped into a floating boat.
Most woods are between half as dense as water and nearly as dense, so they float.
Cooking oil is about nine tenths as dense as water, so oil floats on water.
explanations.art: A bar chart of density: cork, wood, oil, ice, water, aluminium and iron, with a line marking water, and bars below the line labelled floats, above labelled sinks.

explanations.definition: Upthrust is the upward push of a liquid on anything in it. It equals the weight of the liquid that the thing pushes aside.
explanations.description: Water pushes in every direction on a thing sitting in it, but the push from below is stronger than the push from above. The difference is the upthrust. Push an empty bottle under the water in a bucket, and you can feel the upthrust on your hand. The deeper the bottle goes, the more water it pushes aside, up to the point where it is all under the water. A thing floats when its upthrust can grow big enough to equal its own weight. If the upthrust can never grow that big, even with the whole thing under the water, the thing sinks. This rule is called Archimedes' principle.
examples: A floating boat sits down in the water until the upthrust equals the weight of the boat and its cargo.
A rock feels lighter when you lift it under water, because the upthrust does part of the lifting.
A person feels almost weightless in a swimming pool.
explanations.art: A boat floating on water with a downward arrow labelled weight and an upward arrow labelled upthrust, both the same length.

explanations.concept: Why shape matters: a hollow boat holds air
explanations.definition: A hollow shape that holds air pushes aside more water than a solid lump of the same material. If it pushes aside enough water, the shape floats.
explanations.description: Foil is denser than water, so a ball of foil sinks. When you fold the same foil into a boat, it holds a big space of air. The air weighs almost nothing. The boat and the air together take up a lot of room, and push aside a lot of water. Overall, the boat is light for its size, so it floats. A steel ship floats for the same reason. Most of a ship's hull is air. The hull of a loaded cargo ship, steel, cargo and air together, is less dense than water. If a ship's hull is cracked open and fills with water, the air is replaced, and the ship sinks.
examples: A foil ball sinks, but a foil boat floats.
A steel katori floats when it is set on the water with its mouth up, but it sinks when it fills with water.
A steel ship floats because most of its hull is air.
explanations.art: Two drawings side by side: a solid steel block sinking and a hollow steel boat floating, with the hollow part drawn as a pocket of air.

explanations.concept: Salt water holds things up better
explanations.definition: Salty water is denser than fresh water, because the dissolved salt adds mass without adding much volume.
explanations.description: When salt dissolves in water, the salt particles fit in between the water particles. The mass goes up, but the volume barely changes. So salty water is heavier for its size. Sea water is about 3 out of every 100 parts salt, and is a little denser than river water. A thing that sinks in fresh water may float in very salty water. This is why it is easier to float in the sea than in a swimming pool. The Dead Sea, in the Middle East, is about ten times saltier than the ocean. People can lie back and read a newspaper there. Ships also sit higher in the sea than in a river.
examples: A raw potato sinks in plain water and floats in very salty water.
A swimmer floats more easily in the sea than in a swimming pool.
A ship sits higher in the sea than in a river.
explanations.art: Two glasses side by side, one with plain water and a potato at the bottom, and one with very salty water and the potato floating at the top.

explanations.concept: Why ice floats, and why oil floats
explanations.definition: Ice floats on water because ice is less dense than liquid water. Oil floats on water because oil is less dense than water.
explanations.description: Almost every other solid is denser than its own liquid, so it sinks in it. Ice is different. When water freezes, the water particles lock into an open pattern with gaps between them. The same amount of water takes up more space as ice, about one tenth more, and so ice is less dense. About nine tenths of a floating iceberg is under the water, and one tenth is above. In winter, ice forms on top of a lake, and the water underneath stays liquid, which lets fish survive. Oil floats because oil is less dense than water, and the two do not mix, so oil forms a layer on top.
examples: An ice cube floats in a glass of water, with a little of it above the surface.
Cooking oil forms a layer on top of water in a dal that has been too oily.
Ponds in cold places freeze from the top, and fish live under the ice.
explanations.art: An iceberg with one tenth above the water and nine tenths below, with a label at the waterline.

explanations.definition: Liquids that do not mix will sit in layers, with the densest liquid at the bottom and the least dense at the top.
explanations.description: If you pour oil, water and thick sugar syrup into a glass, they sit one above the other. The syrup is the densest, so it sinks to the bottom. Oil is the least dense, so it floats at the top. Water sits in the middle. Each liquid floats on the liquid that is denser than itself, and sinks in the liquids that are less dense than itself. The layers stay separate for a long time if they are poured gently. A small solid thing dropped into the glass sinks through the layers that are less dense than it is, and stops on the layer that is denser than it is.
examples: Honey sinks to the bottom of a glass of water.
Oil floats on top of water.
A drop of ink in water slowly spreads, but a drop of oil stays together.
explanations.art: A tall glass with three layers: dark syrup at the bottom, yellow water in the middle, and clear oil at the top.

explanations.concept: Fish, submarines and balloons change how dense they are
explanations.definition: To rise or sink, a fish, a submarine or a balloon changes how dense it is overall, by changing how much gas or water it holds.
explanations.description: Many fish have a swim bladder, a bag of gas inside their body. A fish that wants to rise puts more gas into the bag, and becomes lighter for her size. A fish that wants to sink lets gas out. Sharks have no swim bladder. They stay up by swimming and by having a large liver full of oil, which is less dense than water. A submarine has big ballast tanks. To dive, the crew lets water in, which makes the submarine heavier. To rise, they push the water out with compressed air. A hot air balloon rises because the heated air inside is less dense than the cooler air around it.
examples: A rohu fish adds or removes gas in her swim bladder to stay at the right depth.
A submarine fills its tanks with water to sink.
A hot air balloon rises when the burner heats the air inside it.
explanations.art: A cut-away of a submarine with ballast tanks full of water, and next to it a fish with a gas-filled bladder drawn in silver.

explanations.concept: Boats of India and the load line
explanations.definition: A boat is built to hold air and push aside water. A load line is painted on a ship to show how deep it may sit when it carries cargo.
explanations.description: People in India have built boats from whatever floats and is easy to find. At Hogenakkal, on the Kaveri, and at Hampi, on the Tungabhadra, people cross the river in round woven boats called coracles, or parisal in Tamil. A coracle is a wide, shallow basket of bamboo, covered with a waterproof sheet. In Assam, people use rafts of banana stems, which are full of air spaces and float high. Every loaded boat sits lower in the water. If it takes on too much cargo, water reaches the rim and the boat sinks. Large ships have a load line, painted on their side, which shows how low they may safely sit. The mark has different lines for sea water and fresh water.
examples: A coracle on the Kaveri is round, wide and shallow.
A banana-stem raft floats because the stems are full of air spaces.
A ship's load line sits lower on the hull for sea water than for fresh river water.
explanations.art: A coracle with two people crossing a wide river, and next to it a ship's hull with a painted load line.

explanations.definition: A hydrometer is a weighted tube that floats upright in a liquid. The denser the liquid, the higher the tube floats.
explanations.description: A hydrometer floats lower in a liquid that is less dense and higher in a liquid that is denser. A scale on the tube lets you read the density. Dairies use hydrometers to check milk, and car garages use them to check batteries. A letter from about the year 400 CE, written by a man named Synesius, asks Hypatia of Alexandria, a teacher of mathematics and philosophy, to have a hydroscope made for him. This was a tube that floated at different heights in different liquids. Historians are not sure whether she built it. In the activity, you make your own, from a drinking straw.
examples: A milk hydrometer floats lower in milk mixed with water, because the mixture is less dense.
A tube with clay in the bottom floats upright in a glass of water.
The same tube floats higher in salty water.
explanations.art: A tall glass tube with a scale on it floating upright in a jar of liquid, with a second tube floating higher in a jar of salty water.

agreed.text: A thing floats in a liquid when it is less dense than the liquid, and sinks when it is denser.
agreed.evidence: The masses and volumes of many materials have been measured, and their float and sink tests match.

agreed.text: The upthrust on a thing in a liquid equals the weight of the liquid the thing pushes aside.
agreed.evidence: If you weigh the water spilled from a full container, it equals the loss of weight you feel.

agreed.text: A hollow shape that holds air can float even when it is made of a material that sinks.
agreed.evidence: A foil ball sinks and a foil boat floats, and steel ships float.

agreed.text: Salty water is denser than fresh water, so things float higher in it.
agreed.evidence: Ships carry load lines marked for sea water and fresh water, because they sit at different depths.

agreed.text: Ice is less dense than liquid water, so it floats.
agreed.evidence: Ice cubes float, and icebergs float with about a tenth of their volume above the water.

agreed.text: Fish and submarines rise and sink by changing their overall density.
agreed.evidence: Scientists have measured gas in swim bladders, and submarines are built with ballast tanks.

challenging.claim: Heavy things sink and light things float.
challenging.who: Many people, and many young children.
challenging.for: Many heavy things, such as stones and nails, sink. Many light things, such as leaves, float.
challenging.against: A loaded steel ship weighs far more than a pebble and floats. A tiny steel pin or a coin sinks. What matters is how heavy a thing is for its size.

challenging.claim: The shape of a thing alone decides whether it floats.
challenging.who: Aristotle, an ancient Greek thinker, taught that broad, flat things float because of their shape.
challenging.for: A flat foil boat floats and a foil ball sinks.
challenging.against: Shape matters because it changes how much water is pushed aside and how much air is held. A flat solid steel sheet still sinks. Both the material and the shape count.

challenging.claim: A thing needs air inside it to float.
challenging.for: Boats, bottles and balloons float because of the air they hold.
challenging.against: A solid block of wood or a lump of ice floats with no air pocket at all, because the material itself is less dense than water.

challenging.claim: Salt makes water thicker, and that is why things float better in it.
challenging.for: Salty water feels a little heavier or thicker to move through.
challenging.against: Floating depends on density, not on how thick a liquid feels. Salt makes water denser, and that is what lifts a potato.

challenging.claim: Icebergs are mostly under water because ice is heavy.
challenging.for: Most of an iceberg is out of sight under the water.
challenging.against: Ice is lighter than water, not heavier. An iceberg sits mostly under the water because ice is only a little lighter than sea water. If it were much lighter, it would sit higher.

big_questions.q: Floating and sinking also happens in air. Where have you seen it?

big_questions.hint: Think about how people learn from trying, again and again.

big_questions.q: When you lie on your back in the water, who is holding you up?
big_questions.hint: Think about the water, the air in your lungs and your own body.

story.title: The Line on the Ferry
story.note: A made-up story. The science in it is real. A loaded boat sits lower in the water. If too much cargo pushes the rim down to the water, water comes in and the boat sinks. A painted load mark shows how low a boat may safely sit.
text: Rupjyoti lived on Majuli, a big island in the Brahmaputra river in Assam. Every morning, she crossed the river on a ferry to go to school. The ferry was an old wooden boat, painted blue, and the ferryman was Bhaben Da.
Along the side of the boat, Bhaben Da had painted a thin white line. Rupjyoti had never asked what it was for.

In Class 4, her teacher, Mrs Baruah, gave the class a challenge. Each child made a small boat from foil and counted how many coins it could carry before it sank. Rupjyoti's boat carried thirty-one coins. She watched the boat sit lower in the water with every coin. At the thirty-second coin, water poured over the edge, and the boat sank to the bottom of the tub.
'Every boat has a last coin,' said Mrs Baruah. 'The more it carries, the lower it sits. When the water reaches the rim, it comes in.'

The next morning at the river, the ferry was full. Bhaben Da was loading sacks of rice and vegetables for the market, as well as the children. There were so many sacks that the white line was just under the water.
'Bhaben Da,' said Rupjyoti, 'the white line is wet.'
He laughed. 'This boat has carried more than this. She has been crossing this river for twenty years.'

'But look.' Rupjyoti pointed at the water just below the rim. 'In school, my foil boat floated until the water reached the edge. Then it sank, even though it had been fine before. Every coin made it sit lower. What if the last sack is your last coin?'
Bhaben Da looked at the white line. Then he looked at the water, only a hand's width from the rim. The river was rough that day, and small waves slapped against the side.
'What does the line mean, then?' asked Rupjyoti.
Bhaben Da rubbed his chin. 'My father painted it. He said, when the water touches the line, take something off.'
'Then it is a last-coin line,' said Rupjyoti. 'It is where the boat should stop.'

Bhaben Da took off four sacks of rice and left them on the bank. The boat rose in the water until the white line was clear of the river again. 'The rice can go on the second trip,' he said. 'Thank you, Rupjyoti.'

She smiled. On the way across, she watched the water slide past, a good hand's width below the rim, and she thought about all the water the boat was pushing aside. It pushed aside exactly as much as it weighed. No more, and no less.
On the second trip, the rice came across, and the line stayed dry the whole way.
story.epiphany: A boat floats by pushing aside water that weighs as much as the boat. Add more cargo, and it sits lower, until the water reaches the rim.

roots.context: We have tested boats, potatoes and bottles, and learned what makes things float. Now we ask what floating tells us about things, and about ourselves.

deep_truth.truth: In the salt test, the same potato sank in tap water and floated in salty water. The potato had not changed at all. The liquid had. So floating describes the potato and the liquid together.
deep_truth.habit: We say 'this floats' and 'that sinks' as if floating were a trait inside the thing, like its colour. That leaves out the liquid.
deep_truth.evidence: In the salt test, the potato piece, the glass and the amount of water stayed the same. Only the salt changed, and the potato rose from the bottom to the top. If your own results differ, write them down as they are and test again.

three.who_am_i: You float more easily in the sea than in a swimming pool. What you can do depends partly on what is around you.
three.what_is_life: A rohu fish adds or removes gas in her swim bladder, so she can stay at the depth she wants. Many living beings change themselves to suit the water or air around them.
three.what_is_this_world: Ships, fish, ice and balloons each find their place where their own density meets the density of what is around them.

roots.thread: Every floating thing is in a balance. Its weight pulls down, and the liquid pushes up, and the two are equal. Nothing holds the thing up from outside. When the liquid changes, the balance moves to a new place. A ship sits higher in the sea than in a river. Each thing finds its level by meeting what is around it.

teachings.teaching: The best is like water. Water helps all things and does not push to be first. It settles in low places that people avoid.
teachings.link: Water holds up the heaviest ship without any effort. It pushes up exactly as much as the ship weighs, and no more.

teachings.teaching: Nagarjuna, an Indian Buddhist teacher of about the 2nd century CE, taught that things do not have a fixed nature of their own. What a thing is depends on the conditions around it.
teachings.link: A potato is not a floater or a sinker by itself. It depends on the liquid it is in.

science.text: Archimedes' principle: the upthrust on a thing in a liquid equals the weight of the liquid it pushes aside.
Water has dozens of unusual properties, including the fact that ice floats. Scientists still debate the reasons for some of them.

other_view.view: Density is a property of the material alone, like its colour or its hardness. Whether a thing floats then follows from comparing two numbers, the density of the thing and of the liquid. Nothing more needs to be said about relationships.

practice.title: Feel the water push back
practice.say: Fill a big bowl with water and let it go still. Hold an empty, closed bottle in your hands. Push the bottle slowly down into the water, and feel the water pushing back. Breathe in slowly three times. Then let go, and watch the bottle rise to where it rests. Think about how the water and the bottle find their balance.
practice.kid: Push an empty closed bottle down in a bowl of water. Feel the water push back. Breathe in slowly three times. Let go and watch.

ask: Is 'floats' something that a potato has, or something that happens between the potato and the water?
A ship sits higher in the sea than in a river. Has the ship changed?
What other words, such as heavy, big or fast, only make sense when you compare one thing with another?
