items.b: Floats. A coconut has a lot of air inside its shell and husk.

items.f: A brick is dropped into water.
items.b: Sinks. A brick is denser than water.

items.f: A closed, empty plastic bottle is put into water.
items.b: Floats. The air inside makes the bottle lighter than the water it pushes aside.

items.f: The same bottle is filled with sand and closed.
items.b: Sinks. The sand makes the bottle denser than water.

items.f: A helium balloon is let go in a room.
items.b: Floats. Helium is about seven times lighter than air, so the balloon rises.

items.f: The burner of a hot air balloon is switched on.
items.b: Floats. The heated air inside is less dense than the cooler air outside, so the balloon rises.

items.f: A submarine lets sea water into its ballast tanks.
items.b: Sinks. The water makes the submarine heavier overall.

items.f: A submarine pushes the water out of its ballast tanks with compressed air.
items.b: Floats. The submarine becomes lighter overall, so it rises.

items.f: A fish lets gas out of her swim bladder.
items.b: Sinks. She becomes a little denser, so she goes down.

items.f: A steel katori is placed gently on water with its mouth facing up.
items.b: Floats. The katori holds a big space of air and pushes aside enough water.

items.f: A raft of banana stems is set on a river.
items.b: Floats. Banana stems are full of air spaces, so they are much less dense than water.

items.f: A one-rupee coin is dropped into water.
items.b: Sinks. Steel is almost 8 times denser than water.

printables.title: 8 tokens: four that say Floats or rises, and four that say Sinks

rules: One player is the reader. The reader takes the top card and reads the front aloud. The reader does not show the back.
Every other player puts one token face down. Then everyone turns the tokens over together.
The reader reads the back. Every player whose token matches the first word of the back scores one point.
A player who also says why, using the words density, air or salt in a correct reason, scores one more point. The reader decides, using the back of the card.
With two players, the parent and the child swap roles after every card. The reader never guesses on their own card.
After each card, the reader's job passes to the player on the left.
The game ends when all 24 cards have been read. The player with the most points wins. If there is a tie, the tied players share the win.

flow.do: Cut out the 24 cards and the 8 tokens. Shuffle the cards and put them in a pile. Give each player one token of each kind.
flow.say: These cards show things in water or air. Each player gets two tokens. Floats or rises, and Sinks. We will guess what happens to each thing.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards and tokens. Shuffle the cards. Each player takes two tokens.
flow.context: This is the first step of Harbour Master. You set up the cards and the tokens.
flow.parent: One child with a parent: play as the two-player rule says, swapping the reader after every card. Two to four children: use all the tokens. If the group is short of time, play 16 cards and stop.

flow.do: Play the first six cards. After each card, read the back aloud. After card three, ask the question below.
flow.say: The reader reads the front. Everyone else chooses a token. Turn the tokens over together. Now the reader reads the back. Who got a point? Who can say why?
flow.kid: The reader reads a card. Pick a token. Turn it over. Check the back.

ask.q: What do the things that float have in common?
good: They are lighter than water for their size.
They are less dense than water.

flow.context: In this step, you play the first six cards and learn how to score.

flow.do: Play the next eight cards. Swap the reader's job after every card. Keep a tally of points on paper.
flow.say: Keep going. Remember what decides floating. Is it lighter than the same amount of water? Does it hold air? Is the water salty?
flow.kid: Play on. Is it lighter than the same amount of water? Does it hold air?

ask.q: Which card surprised you so far, and why?
good: The potato floats in salt water.

flow.context: In this step, you play the middle of the game and keep score.

flow.do: Play the last ten cards. When the pile is finished, count each player's points.
flow.say: Last cards. Think about the density of the thing and the density of what is around it.
flow.kid: Play the last cards. Count your points.
flow.context: In this step, you finish the pile of cards and count the points.

flow.do: Say who won. Ask your child which card was the hardest to guess, and why.
flow.say: Who got the most points? Which card was hardest? Why was it hard?
flow.kid: Who won? Which card was hardest? Why?
flow.think: Which card would change if the liquid were different?
flow.context: This is the last step of Harbour Master. You look back at the game.

games.safety: Use blunt-ended scissors for the cards, and an adult should cut for children under six.

experiments.title: Foil Boats: which shape carries the most coins?
experiments.question: A foil ball sinks. Which foil boat shape carries the most coins before it sinks: a wide, shallow one, a medium one, or a narrow, deep one?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Which boat will carry the most coins? Which will carry the fewest? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Every boat is made from a square of foil of the same size. The basin and the depth of the water are the same for every test. You add coins in the same way each time, gently and one at a time. Only the shape of the boat changes, so any difference comes from the shape. The foil ball is the control. It shows what happens to the same foil with no hollow shape.

materials.item: 4 squares of kitchen foil, each exactly 15 centimetres by 15 centimetres
a ruler and a pair of scissors (blunt-ended ones are fine; foil cuts easily)
a big basin or bucket, at least 25 centimetres wide, with water about 10 centimetres deep
about 60 identical coins, such as one-rupee coins (each weighs about 4 to 5 grams), or about 60 identical steel nuts or washers
a towel for wiping up spills
the results table and a pencil

experiments.safety: Fold the foil edges over, because cut foil can be sharp. Keep coins and nuts away from children under five, who might put them in their mouths. Wipe up spilt water at once so nobody slips.
experiments.record: For each boat, write how many coins it carried before it tipped or water came over the rim. Do each boat twice. Then draw a bar chart with one bar for each boat, using the bigger of the two numbers.
experiments.context: In this experiment, you fold the same foil into three different boats and find out how many coins each can carry. You also test a ball of foil.

setup.art: A square of foil on a table with a ruler, and the four edges being folded up by 1 centimetre, 3 centimetres and 5 centimetres into three different trays.
setup.caption: 1. Fold three foil squares into boats: wide and shallow, medium, and narrow and deep.

setup.art: A fourth square of foil being squeezed into a ball and set beside the three boats.
setup.caption: 2. Squeeze the fourth square into a ball. This is the control.

setup.art: A basin of water with a foil boat floating in the middle and a pile of coins beside the basin.
setup.caption: 3. Float the first boat in the middle of the basin.

setup.art: A child's hand placing one coin gently into the centre of a floating foil boat, with a count of coins written beside it.
setup.caption: 4. Add coins gently, one at a time, in the middle. Count each one.

setup.art: A foil boat tipped to one side with water pouring over its rim and coins sliding into the basin.
setup.caption: 5. When the boat tips or water comes over the rim, stop and write the number.

flow.do: Show your child the foil, the basin and the coins. Say that all three boats are made from the same size of foil. Write down their guess and their reason.
flow.say: We will fold three boats from the same size of foil. One is wide and shallow. One is medium. One is narrow and deep. We will also squeeze one square into a ball. Which boat will carry the most coins? Which will carry the fewest? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Three boats from the same foil. One is wide. One is medium. One is deep. Which carries the most coins? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think that boat will carry the most?
good: It will push aside the most water.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is a good start. Write the guesses at the top of the table. One child with a parent: the child folds and loads, the parent counts aloud and writes. Two to four children: each child folds and tests one boat (a different one each), then compares; one child is the counter, one adds coins, one writes. Make one set of boats per pair so every boat is tested twice. Nothing here needs more than one adult.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Foil Boats test. You guess before you test.

flow.do: Measure and cut four squares of foil, each 15 centimetres by 15 centimetres. Fold the first square up 1 centimetre on every side. Fold the second up 3 centimetres on every side. Fold the third up 5 centimetres on every side. Pinch the corners so the sides stand up. Squeeze the fourth into a ball.
flow.say: Fold each edge up, and press the corners to make the sides stand. The first boat has low sides and a wide base. The second has medium sides. The third has tall sides and a narrow base. The fourth is a ball.
flow.kid: Cut four squares of foil. Fold up the edges of three. Make a ball with the last one.
flow.parent: Make the squares exactly the same size. Fold the sharp edges inwards so nobody scratches a finger. Write A, B and C on a small piece of paper by each boat. Fold the four corners flat against the sides and press them hard, so water cannot leak in through the corner folds.

check.q: Why must all four foil squares be the same size?
options: So the foil does not tear
check.why: In a fair test, only one thing changes. If one square were bigger, you would not know whether the shape or the size made the difference.

flow.context: In this step, you fold the boats. They are all made from the same size of foil.

flow.do: Fill the basin with water about 10 centimetres deep. Put the foil ball in the water, and watch what it does. Then float boat A in the middle of the basin.
flow.say: First, the ball. Put it in gently. What does it do? Now take it out. Float the first boat in the middle of the basin. What is different?
flow.kid: Put the foil ball in the water. What does it do? Now float boat A. What is different?

ask.q: The ball and the boat are the same foil. Why does one sink and the other float?
good: The boat pushes aside more water.

flow.parent: Do not explain yet. Let your child say what they think. The ball should sink straight away. Record 0 coins for the ball.
flow.context: In this step, you try the ball, then the first boat. You see the difference that shape makes.

flow.do: Float boat A in the middle of the basin. Add coins one at a time, gently, into the centre of the boat. Count each coin out loud. Stop when the boat tips or water comes over the rim. Write the number of coins it carried. Dry the boat and do it again. Then test boat B and boat C in the same way.
flow.say: Add the coins one at a time, in the middle, very gently. Count each one. The last coin is the one that makes it fail. Write down the number of coins it carried before that. Then try again, to see if you get the same number.
flow.kid: Add coins one at a time to the boat. Count them. Stop when it tips or sinks. Write the number.

ask.q: What happens to the boat in the water as you add more coins?
good: The water gets close to the edge.

flow.parent: Coins go in the middle. Stack them in small piles as the boat fills. If the boat tips, note it, and try again. Your numbers may differ between tries. That is normal, and it is why we do each boat twice. If you run out of coins before a boat fails, write 'more than 60' and add heavier items such as two-rupee or five-rupee coins. Foil boats are fussy: the numbers are likely to differ by several coins between tries, and that is normal.

check.q: Boat A carries 24 coins on try 1 and 26 coins on try 2. What does this show?
options: The result is steady, so we can trust it
check.why: Two results that are close together show the test gives about the same answer every time. If they were very different, we could not trust either one.

flow.context: In this step, you load each boat with coins until it fails. You count carefully.

flow.do: Draw a bar chart with one bar for each boat. Use the bigger of the two numbers. Then ask your child to say what they thought, what they saw and why.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What did you think would happen? What did you see? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Draw a bar for each boat. Say what you thought, what you saw, and why.
flow.think: Why did the ball of foil sink but every boat float?
flow.parent: A strong answer says that the boat with the most room for air pushed aside the most water. By the volume of water each boat can hold, the medium boat should carry the most, and the narrow deep boat the fewest. But a tall boat can tip, and a wide shallow boat can fill over its low rim, so the order in your basin may differ. The pattern is not promised. Write what you actually saw, and give a reason for it. After they have said what they saw, explain: each cubic centimetre of water pushed aside weighs one gram. The boat can carry cargo until the water it pushes aside weighs as much as the boat and the cargo together.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Foil Boats test. You draw the chart and explain what you found.

experiments.title: The Potato and the Salt: when does it float?
experiments.question: A raw potato sinks in plain water. How much salt do you need to add to a glass of water before the potato floats?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. How many tablespoons of salt will it take before the potato floats? Will it ever float? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: You use the same piece of potato, the same glass and the same amount of water every time. You add one level tablespoon of salt at a time, and stir until it disappears. Only the amount of salt changes, so any change in the potato comes from the salt. The plain water at the start is the control.
results_table: Does the potato sink, hover or float?
Where is the potato: bottom, middle or top?

materials.item: a clear tall glass or jar that holds about 400 millilitres, so there is room for the salt
250 millilitres of tap water, measured with a cup
one piece of raw potato about 2 centimetres across, about the size of a walnut
about 5 level tablespoons of table salt (a finer salt dissolves faster)
a spoon for stirring, and a tablespoon for measuring
the results table and a pencil

experiments.record: After every tablespoon of salt, write what the potato does and where it sits. Draw the glass at the start and at the end.
experiments.context: In this experiment, you find out what happens to a potato in water as you add salt a spoon at a time.

setup.art: A tall glass with 250 millilitres of tap water and a piece of raw potato resting at the bottom.
setup.caption: 1. Put the potato in plain water. It sinks.

setup.art: A level tablespoon of salt being stirred into the glass of water, with the potato lifted out on a spoon.
setup.caption: 2. Take the potato out. Stir in one level tablespoon of salt until it disappears.

setup.art: The potato being lowered gently back into the salty water, with a close-up of whether it sinks, hovers or floats.
setup.caption: 3. Put the potato back. Does it sink, hover or float?

setup.art: Three glasses in a row showing the potato at the bottom, in the middle and at the top, as more and more salt is added.
setup.caption: 4. Keep adding one spoon at a time. Write down what the potato does.

flow.do: Show your child the glass, the potato and the salt. Ask for a guess and a reason. Write the guess at the top of the table.
flow.say: We have a potato, a glass of water and some salt. The potato will sink in plain water. What will happen as we add salt? When will it change? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: A potato sinks in plain water. What happens when you add salt? Why do you think so?

ask.q: Why do you think salt might change what the potato does?

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is a good start. One child with a parent: the child adds salt and watches, and the parent counts the spoons and writes. Two to four children: give each child a glass and a piece of potato cut from the same potato; one child can test an egg instead of a potato (a raw egg usually floats after about 2 to 3 tablespoons, but yours may differ). Compare when they float.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Potato and the Salt test. You guess before you test.

flow.do: Pour 250 millilitres of tap water into the glass. Put the potato in gently. Watch it sink. Write 0 spoons in the first row of the table, and write what the potato does.
flow.say: Put the potato in gently. What does it do? This is our plain water test, with no salt.
flow.kid: Fill the glass with 250 millilitres of water. Put the potato in. What does it do?
flow.parent: The potato should sink to the bottom. Most raw potatoes do. If yours floats in plain water, use a different piece, from the middle of a bigger potato.
flow.context: In this step, you test the potato in plain water, before any salt. This is the control.

flow.do: Take the potato out with a spoon. Add one level tablespoon of salt. Stir for about a minute, until the salt disappears. Put the potato back gently. Write what it does. Repeat, adding one tablespoon at a time, up to 5 tablespoons in all or until the potato floats.
flow.say: Take the potato out first. Add one level tablespoon of salt, and stir until you can't see it. Put the potato back. Does it sink, hover or float? Do this again with another spoon.
flow.kid: Take out the potato. Add one spoon of salt. Stir. Put the potato back. Write what it does. Repeat.

ask.q: What do you notice about the potato as you add more salt?

flow.parent: Hovering is when the potato stays in the middle of the glass and neither sinks nor floats. This tells you the salty water is about as dense as the potato. Many potatoes float after about 2 to 4 tablespoons, but this is typical, not promised. A new, watery potato may need more, and an old one less. If salt stays at the bottom after a minute of stirring, the water cannot hold more. If the potato still sinks at 5 tablespoons, try a thinner slice of potato or a different potato: salt only changes the water, and some potatoes are denser than any salt water you can make. Stir warm tap water (not hot) if the salt is slow to dissolve.

check.q: After 3 tablespoons of salt, the potato floats. What has changed?
check.why: The potato is the same piece, so its density has not changed. The salt made the water heavier for its size, and denser than the potato.

flow.context: In this step, you add salt one spoon at a time and watch the potato.

flow.do: Ask your child to say what they thought, what they saw and why. Then look at the table and find the row where the potato first changed. Pour the salty water down the sink and wash the glass.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What did you think would happen? What did you see? Why do you think it happened? When did the potato first change?
flow.kid: Say what you thought, what you saw, and why. When did the potato first change?
flow.think: The potato did not change. What did?
flow.parent: A strong answer says that the potato was the same and that the salty water was denser. After they have said what they saw, explain: salt dissolves in the water and makes it heavier for its size. When the water is denser than the potato, the potato floats. This is also why it is easier to float in the sea than in a swimming pool.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Potato and the Salt test. You explain what you found.

experiments.safety: Salty water is not for drinking. Wash hands after handling the raw potato. If you try an egg, wipe up any broken egg at once.

activities.title: Guess and Sort: ten things from the kitchen

materials.item: a big bowl or bucket of water
a steel spoon, a wooden spoon, a one-rupee coin, a lemon (with its skin on), a whole raw potato, a candle stub, a plastic bottle cap
a small empty plastic bottle with a cap, and a steel katori
paper with two columns, and a pencil

schedule.what: Guess for each thing. Test each one. Sort them. Look for a pattern, and find where it breaks.

activities.record: A table with ten things, your guess for each, what happened, and a final sort into floats and sinks.
activities.context: In this activity, you guess whether ten things float or sink, test them, and look for a pattern. Then you test the pattern.

setup.art: Ten kitchen things in a row beside a bowl of water: a steel spoon, wooden spoon, coin, lemon, potato, candle stub, bottle cap, closed bottle and two katoris.
setup.caption: 1. Line up the ten things. Guess for each one.

setup.art: A child dropping a steel spoon into a bowl of water, and a wooden spoon floating beside it.
setup.caption: 2. Test each one gently. Write what happens.

setup.art: A sheet of paper with two columns labelled floats and sinks, and small drawings of the things in each column.
setup.caption: 3. Sort the things into two groups.

flow.do: Line up the ten things. They are a steel spoon, a wooden spoon, a coin, a lemon and a potato. Add a candle stub, a bottle cap and a closed empty bottle. The last two are the katori set mouth up, and the katori pushed down until it fills. Write a guess for each: floats or sinks.
flow.say: Look at each thing. Hold it. Will it float or sink? Write your guess for each one before we test.
flow.kid: Look at the ten things. Guess for each one. Float or sink? Write it down.

ask.q: Which do you think is the hardest to guess?

flow.parent: Do not correct the guesses. Any guess is fine. The last two items are the same steel katori, set on the water mouth up, and then pushed under until it fills. One child with a parent: take turns, the child guesses first and the parent second. Two to four children: each child writes their own guesses on their own table, then tests the items in turn; compare who guessed most right.
flow.context: This is the first step of Guess and Sort. You guess before you test.

flow.do: Test the things one at a time. Lower each one gently into the water. Write down what happens. Keep the katori for last. Set it on the water mouth up. Then push it under so it fills with water.
flow.say: Gently, one at a time. What happens? Does it match your guess? For the katori, first it sits on the water. Then we push it down until it fills. What changes?
flow.kid: Test each thing in the water. Write what happens. Did you guess right?
flow.parent: Expected: the steel spoon, coin and potato sink. The wooden spoon, candle stub, bottle cap and closed bottle float. A lemon with its skin on usually floats (a peeled one may sink). Wood and candle wax can differ a little; write down what yours does, because your own result counts. The katori floats mouth up and sinks when it fills. If something differs, write it down.

check.q: The steel katori floats when set on the water mouth up, and sinks when it fills with water. What changed?
options: The air inside was replaced by water
check.why: The steel is the same. When the katori filled, the air pocket that helped it float was replaced by water, which made the katori sink.

flow.context: In this step, you test each thing and write what happens.

flow.do: Sort the ten things into two columns: floats and sinks. Ask your child to look for a pattern. Then ask whether the pattern is always true.
flow.say: Look at the two columns. Is there a pattern? Is it always the heavy things that sink? What about the steel katori, which is heavy but floats?
flow.kid: Sort the things into floats and sinks. Is there a pattern? Is it always true?

ask.q: Is it true that heavy things sink and light things float?
good: No. The katori is heavy but floats.
No. The coin is small but sinks.
It depends on the shape and what it is made of.

flow.parent: A good pattern to test: heavy things sink. The katori breaks it. A better pattern: a thing floats if it is lighter than the water it pushes aside.
flow.context: In this step, you sort the things and look for a pattern. Then you test the pattern.

flow.do: Ask your child to say what they thought, what they saw and why. Pour the water back, and dry the things.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What did you think would happen? What did you see? Why did the katori float when it held air, and sink when it held water?
flow.kid: Say what you thought, what you saw, and why.
flow.think: How would you test the pattern 'wooden things always float'?
flow.context: This is the last step of Guess and Sort. You explain what you found.
flow.parent: Count how many of the ten guesses were right, and write the score on the table. Count the katori twice, once for each way.

activities.safety: Coins, bottle caps and nuts are small parts: keep them from children under five. Wipe up spilt water so nobody slips.

activities.title: Density Tower: three liquids that will not mix

materials.item: a tall clear glass or jar that holds about 300 millilitres
4 tablespoons of sugar and about 4 tablespoons of warm water
a few drops of food colour (or a pinch of turmeric) for the syrup, and a few drops of a different colour for the water if you have one
about 100 millilitres of plain water
about 100 millilitres of cooking oil
a spoon, and a cup or jug for pouring
a few tiny things from the kitchen to drop in at the end, such as a peppercorn, a grain of rice, a raisin, a small piece of candle

schedule.what: Make the sugar syrup. Pour the three layers. Look at the tower and explain it. Drop in small things to see which layer they stop in.

activities.record: Draw the glass with three layers, and label each layer. Write which liquid is the densest and which is the least dense.
activities.context: In this activity, you pour three liquids into a glass. You watch them stay in layers and find out which is densest.

setup.art: A spoon of sugar being stirred into warm water in a cup, with a drop of colour added.
setup.caption: 1. Stir sugar into warm water to make a thick coloured syrup.

setup.art: A glass with the syrup at the bottom, and plain water being poured slowly over the back of a spoon on top.
setup.caption: 2. Pour the water slowly over the back of a spoon.

setup.art: A glass with three clear layers, syrup at the bottom, water in the middle and oil on top.
setup.caption: 3. Pour the oil the same way. Look at the three layers.

flow.do: Ask your child to guess which liquid will be at the top, which in the middle and which at the bottom. Then stir the sugar into the warm water, until no grains are left. Add a drop of colour. Let it cool for a few minutes.
flow.say: We have three liquids: sugar syrup, plain water and cooking oil. Which will end up on the top? Which will end up at the bottom? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess the order of the three liquids. Why do you think so? Stir sugar into warm water.

ask.q: Why do you think that liquid will be at the bottom?

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Make the syrup thick, with as much sugar as dissolves. One child with a parent: the child pours, the parent steadies the glass. Two to four children: make one tower per pair, so every child gets to pour, and compare towers. If you have only one colour, colour the syrup; the clear water layer will then show between the coloured syrup and the oil.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Density Tower. You guess, and then make the syrup.

flow.do: Pour the syrup slowly into the bottom of the glass. Try not to let it touch the sides.
flow.say: Pour the syrup slowly into the glass. It will stay at the bottom.
flow.kid: Pour the syrup into the glass. Do it slowly.
flow.context: In this step, you pour the first layer, the syrup.

flow.do: Hold a spoon, bowl facing up, just above the syrup. Pour the plain water slowly onto the back of the spoon, so it runs gently on top of the syrup.
flow.say: Pour the water onto the back of the spoon, so the water runs slowly onto the syrup. A fast pour would mix them.
flow.kid: Pour water slowly over the back of a spoon onto the syrup.
flow.parent: Some mixing at the line between the layers is normal. Pour more slowly, or make the syrup thicker, and try again. Use a tall narrow glass, because a wide one is harder to pour into neatly. Over a few hours the syrup and water slowly blend at the edge. That is normal too.
flow.context: In this step, you pour the second layer, the plain water.

flow.do: Pour the cooking oil slowly over the back of the spoon, onto the water. Put the glass on a table and leave it still.
flow.say: Now the oil, over the back of the spoon. Then leave the glass still.
flow.kid: Pour oil slowly over the spoon. Leave the glass still.
flow.context: In this step, you pour the top layer, the oil.

flow.do: Look at the tower from the side. Draw it and label each layer. Then gently stir the top with the spoon, and watch what the oil does. Drop in a few small things from the kitchen one at a time (a peppercorn, a grain of rice, a raisin). Write which layer each one stops in. Ask your child to say what they thought, what they saw and why.
flow.say: Which layer is on top? Which is at the bottom? Why do you think each liquid is where it is? What happens to the oil when we stir it?
flow.kid: Look at the three layers. Draw them. Stir the top gently. What does the oil do?

check.q: Oil sits on top of water. What does this show about oil?
options: Oil is less dense than water
check.why: A liquid that floats on another liquid is less dense than it is. Thickness is a different idea. Honey is thick, but oil is thin and still floats.

flow.think: What would happen if you poured honey into this glass?
flow.parent: When you stir, the oil breaks into drops and rises back to the top, because it is less dense than the water. The water and the syrup slowly mix. After they have said what they saw, explain: each liquid floats on the one that is denser than itself. You cannot know beforehand which layer each small thing will stop in, and that is the point: it stops where the liquid below is denser than the thing and the liquid above is less dense. Write down what you see.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Density Tower. You look at the layers and explain them.

activities.safety: Use warm tap water, not boiling. An adult should heat the water if it needs heating. Food colour stains clothes. Oil makes the floor slippery, so wipe spills at once. Do not drink the layers, and pour the oil into the dustbin, not the sink.

activities.title: Make a Hydroscope: a floating density meter

materials.item: a plastic drinking straw, as thick as you can find, such as a juice or smoothie straw, cut to about 15 centimetres
a small piece of modelling clay, about the size of a marble
two tall clear glasses
250 millilitres of plain water, and 250 millilitres of water with 4 level tablespoons of salt stirred in until it disappears
a marker pen that writes on plastic, and a ruler
a small steel nut or a few pins, to adjust the weight if needed

schedule.what: Make the hydroscope. Float it in plain water and mark the line. Float it in salty water and mark the line. Compare.

activities.record: Write the length of straw above the water in plain water and in salty water. Draw the hydroscope in each glass.
activities.context: In this activity, you make a floating tube like the hydroscope that Hypatia was asked to build. You use it to compare how dense two liquids are.

setup.art: A drinking straw with a ball of modelling clay pressed into one end, sealing it.
setup.caption: 1. Press clay into one end of the straw, so water cannot get in.

setup.art: A straw floating upright in a tall glass of plain water, with a marker line drawn at the waterline.
setup.caption: 2. Float the straw in plain water. Mark the waterline.

setup.art: The same straw floating higher in a glass of salty water, with a second marker line at the new waterline.
setup.caption: 3. Float it in salty water. Mark the new waterline.

flow.do: Press about a centimetre and a half of clay firmly into one end of the straw, so that the end is sealed. Check that no water can get in.
flow.say: The clay seals one end, and it also makes that end heavy. The heavy end will go down, and the straw will float upright.
flow.kid: Press clay into one end of the straw. Seal it well.
flow.parent: Press the clay in about a finger-nail deep, and smooth it. If the straw leaks later, press more clay in. One child with a parent: the child makes the straw, the parent dries and measures. Two to four children: each child makes their own hydroscope, because every straw floats a little differently, then compares the gap between marks. Use real modelling clay (plasticine), not dough that dissolves in water.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Hydroscope. You make the weighted straw.

flow.do: Fill a glass with plain water. Put the straw in, clay end first. It should float upright with about one third above the water. Add or remove clay, or push in a pin, until it does. Mark the waterline with the marker.
flow.say: The straw should stand upright with some of it above the water. If it lies down, it needs more weight at the bottom. If it sinks, it has too much. Mark the waterline.
flow.kid: Float the straw in plain water. It must stand up. Mark the waterline.

ask.q: What do you think will happen in salty water?

flow.parent: If your straw lies on its side, add a small steel nut or pins at the clay end. If it sinks, take some clay off. A straw of about 15 centimetres with a marble of clay at the bottom is a good start. Nothing exact is promised: a few tries is normal. Do not worry if it takes a few tries.
flow.context: In this step, you float the straw in plain water and mark the waterline.

flow.do: Stir 4 level tablespoons of salt into 250 millilitres of water in the second glass, until the salt disappears. Ask your child to guess whether the straw will float higher or lower. Write the guess.
flow.say: Salty water is denser. Will the straw float higher or lower in it? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Make very salty water. Guess if the straw floats higher or lower. Why?
flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is a good start.
flow.context: In this step, you make salty water and guess what the straw will do.

flow.do: Dry the straw. Put it in the salty water, clay end first. Mark the new waterline. Take it out and measure the distance between the two marks.
flow.say: Where is the waterline now? Is it higher or lower than before? How far has it moved?
flow.kid: Float the straw in salty water. Mark the waterline. Measure the gap between the two marks.

check.q: The straw floats higher in salty water. What does this tell you about salty water?
options: It is denser than plain water
It is less dense than plain water
It is the same as plain water
check.why: A denser liquid pushes up harder on the same straw, so the straw does not need to sink as far. That is how a hydrometer works.

flow.parent: The straw typically floats about one to two centimetres higher in the very salty water. Size depends on your straw. If you see no change, check that the salt really dissolved (all of it must disappear), dry the straw before the second glass, and make sure the clay end is sealed. A thicker straw is easier to read. Salt that stays at the bottom of the glass has not dissolved and does not count.
flow.context: In this step, you float the straw in the salty water and measure the change.

flow.do: Ask your child to say what they thought, what they saw and why. Tell the story of Hypatia and the hydroscope from the card.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What did you think would happen? What did you see? Why do you think it happened? A letter from about 1,600 years ago asks a teacher called Hypatia to build a tube like this.
flow.kid: Say what you thought, what you saw, and why.
flow.think: How could you use your hydroscope to check whether milk has been mixed with water?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Hydroscope. You explain what you found.

activities.safety: Pins are sharp and a steel nut is a small part: an adult should handle the pins, and keep both away from children under five.

projects.title: Bottle Diver: a diver that sinks when you squeeze

materials.item: a thin, clear plastic bottle with a cap, such as a 500 millilitre mineral-water bottle, with smooth sides that squeeze easily (fizzy-drink bottles are too stiff)
a small plastic pen cap (the kind with a clip works well, clear if possible); seal any tiny hole in its top with a speck of clay
a small piece of modelling clay (plasticine), about the size of a marble
a big bowl of water, and a jug
a towel for spills

schedule.what: Make the diver. Test it in a bowl. Put it in the bottle. Squeeze and watch.

projects.record: Draw the bottle with the diver, before and after squeezing. Show the air bubble in each drawing.
projects.context: In this project, you make a small diver that sinks when you squeeze a bottle and rises when you let go. You find out how it works.

setup.art: A pen cap with a small blob of modelling clay stuck on the outside, floating upright in a bowl of water.
setup.caption: 1. Float the pen cap in a bowl. Add clay until it just barely floats.

setup.art: The pen cap diver being slipped into a bottle filled to the brim with water, open end down.
setup.caption: 2. Put the diver in a bottle full of water. Close the cap tight.

setup.art: A hand squeezing the bottle, with the diver sinking, and an arrow showing the air bubble inside getting smaller.
setup.caption: 3. Squeeze the bottle. The diver sinks. Let go. It rises.

flow.do: Show your child the bottle, the pen cap and the clay. Ask for a guess and a reason.
flow.say: We will make a little diver. When we squeeze the bottle, what do you think the diver will do? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: A tiny diver in a bottle. What will it do when you squeeze? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think the diver might sink or rise?
good: The air in it gets squashed.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is a good start. One child with a parent: the child builds the diver, the parent tops up the bottle. Two to four children: each child makes their own diver and bottle, then you race: whose diver sinks first, and can anyone keep it still in the middle?
flow.context: This is the first step of the Bottle Diver. You guess before you build.

flow.do: Seal the tiny hole in the top of the pen cap with a speck of clay, if it has one. Wrap a small ring of clay around the outside of the open end of the cap, so that it floats upright. Put the cap in a bowl of water with the open end down. Add or take off clay until it just floats, with only its top above the water.
flow.say: The air trapped inside the cap makes it float. The clay makes it a little heavier. We want it to float just barely, with only the very top above the water.
flow.kid: Put clay on the pen cap. Float it open end down. Add clay until it barely floats.
flow.parent: If the cap floats too high, add more clay. If it sinks, take a little off. The balance has to be very fine. Do not worry if it takes a few tries. Make sure the open end of the cap faces down, so that air stays trapped inside.
flow.context: In this step, you make the diver and balance it in a bowl.

flow.do: Fill the bottle to the very top with water. Slip the diver in, open end down. Top the bottle up to the brim, so that no air bubble is left. Close the cap tight.
flow.say: The bottle must be full to the brim. There should be no air in the bottle, except the air inside the diver.
flow.kid: Fill the bottle to the top. Put the diver in. Close the cap tight.
flow.context: In this step, you put the diver in the bottle and seal it.

flow.do: Squeeze the sides of the bottle. Watch the diver. Look closely at the air inside the diver while you squeeze. Let go. Watch again. Try different amounts of squeezing.
flow.say: Squeeze slowly. What does the diver do? Look at the bubble of air inside. Is it bigger or smaller when you squeeze? Now let go.
flow.kid: Squeeze the bottle. Watch the diver. Look at the bubble. Let go.

ask.q: What happens to the air bubble when you squeeze?

check.q: When you squeeze the bottle, the diver sinks. Why?
options: The air inside it is squashed, so it pushes aside less water
check.why: Squeezing pushes water into the cap and squashes the air. The diver pushes aside less water, so the upthrust gets smaller and the diver sinks. When you let go, the air springs back and the diver rises.

flow.parent: If the diver does not move, squeeze harder, or take a little clay off. If it sinks and stays down, add a little less clay next time. To make the test measurable, count how many seconds your diver takes to reach the bottom, or try to hold it in the middle of the bottle for ten seconds. A bubble of air left at the top of the bottle makes it hard to squeeze the diver down: top up the bottle to the brim. Some divers never work at first: add or remove a tiny bit of clay and try again.
flow.context: In this step, you squeeze the bottle and watch the diver.

flow.do: Draw the bottle with the diver, before and after squeezing. Show the air bubble in each. Then ask your child to say what they thought, what they saw and why.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What did you think would happen? What did you see? Why do you think it happened? Where do you see this idea in submarines and fish?
flow.kid: Draw the bottle before and after. Say what you thought, what you saw, and why.
flow.think: How is the diver like a submarine, and how is it like a fish?
flow.parent: A strong answer says that squeezing made the air smaller, so the diver pushed aside less water and became denser overall, so it sank. A submarine changes its density with ballast tanks, and a fish with her swim bladder.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Bottle Diver. You draw it and explain what you found.

projects.safety: A pen cap is a small part and clay should not be eaten: keep both from children under five. Wipe up spilt water so nobody slips.

challenges.title: Cargo Ship: carry the most coins with one sheet of foil
challenges.problem: You have one sheet of foil, 20 centimetres by 20 centimetres. Fold it into a boat that carries as many coins as possible across a basin of water, and does not sink for one full minute.
constraints: Use only one square of foil, 20 centimetres by 20 centimetres, with no tape or glue.
The coins must be added one at a time, gently.
The boat must float for one full minute with the load.
Count the coins your boat carries.
materials: a square of kitchen foil, 20 centimetres by 20 centimetres
about 60 identical coins or steel nuts
general: A box shape, with straight sides and a flat base, like the medium boat in the Foil Boats test.
A wide boat with sides that are tall enough to keep the water out.
A boat that keeps its coins in the middle, so it does not tip.
creative: Two narrow hulls side by side, joined by a flat deck, like a catamaran, to keep the boat steady.
A boat with a ridge or a fold across the middle, to keep the sides from folding in.
A boat with rounded sides, like a coracle, that sits low and steady.
challenges.your_turn: Sketch your design. Build it and test it. Change one thing, such as the height of the sides, and test again. Which design carried the most coins? Why do you think it did?
challenges.context: This is a design challenge about shape and floating. You build the best foil cargo ship you can.

setup.art: A child sketching three boat designs on paper: a box, a catamaran with two hulls, and a round coracle.
setup.caption: 1. Sketch some designs on paper.

setup.art: A foil boat being loaded with coins in a basin of water, with a timer running beside it.
setup.caption: 2. Build your boat. Load it with coins, and time one minute.

setup.art: Two boats side by side, one with fifteen coins and one with thirty, with the numbers written below.
setup.caption: 3. Change one thing at a time, and compare.

flow.do: Read the problem together. Look at the constraints. Ask your child to sketch two or three different boat designs.
flow.say: You have one sheet of foil. How could you fold it so that the boat carries the most? Draw some ideas first.
flow.kid: You have one foil sheet. Draw some boat ideas first.

ask.q: What would make a boat carry more?

flow.context: This is the first step of the Cargo Ship challenge. You plan.

flow.do: Build your first design. Float it in the basin. Add coins one at a time, gently. Count them. Keep going until it tips or sinks. Write down the number.
flow.say: Build your first boat. Load it. How many coins does it carry? Write it down, so you have something to beat.
flow.kid: Build your boat. Add coins. Count them. Write the number.
flow.parent: Fold the edges over, so the foil is not sharp. Place the coins in the middle, side by side. This first number is the one to beat.
flow.context: In this step, you build your first design and test it.

flow.do: Change one thing about your design. Test it again with coins. Write down both numbers. Which is better?
flow.say: Change just one thing. Make the sides higher, or the base wider. Test again. Is it better or worse?
flow.kid: Change one thing. Test again. Is it better or worse?

ask.q: Why do you think that change made it better, or worse?

flow.context: In this step, you improve your design, changing only one thing at a time.

flow.do: Test your best boat once more, and time one full minute with the load. Write down the final number of coins. Compare with your first try.
flow.say: This is the final test. Load your best boat and wait one minute. Did it float? How many coins did it carry? How is it different from your first?
flow.kid: Test your best boat for one minute. Write the number of coins.
flow.think: What would you change if you had one more sheet of foil?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Cargo Ship challenge. You do the final test.

items.p: Which is the best reason a big steel ship floats?
opts: Most of its hull is air, so the ship is lighter than the water it pushes aside
Steel is lighter than water
The sea is always pushing the ship up by magic
items.why: Steel itself is much denser than water. But a ship is a hollow shape full of air. The whole ship, steel and air together, is lighter than the water it pushes aside.

items.p: What does the word density tell you about a material?
opts: How much stuff is packed into a certain space
How hot the material is
How shiny the material is
items.why: Density is mass divided by volume. A dense material is heavy for its size.

items.p: A heavy thing always sinks in water.
items.why: False. A loaded steel ship is very heavy and floats, because it pushes aside a huge amount of water. What matters is how heavy a thing is for its size.

items.p: The upward push of water on a thing in it is called ____.
items.why: Upthrust is the push up from a liquid. It gets bigger as more of the thing goes under the water.

items.p: Match each material to what it does in water.
pairs: Cooking oil
floats on top of the water
Honey
sinks to the bottom
Ice
floats, with a little above the surface
Iron nail
sinks
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Oil is less dense than water, so it floats. Honey and iron are denser than water, so they sink. Ice is a little less dense than liquid water, so it floats.

items.p: Sort each thing by what it does in plain water.
items.a: as given
items.why: Wood, lemon, candle wax and a bottle full of air are lighter than the same amount of water, so they float. Steel, a potato, a coin and a brick are heavier, so they sink.

items.p: A ball of foil sinks, but a foil boat made from the same foil floats. Why?
opts: The boat holds air and pushes aside more water
The boat is made of lighter foil
Water likes boats better than balls
items.why: The foil is the same, but the boat has a hollow shape with air in it. It pushes aside much more water than the ball does, so the upthrust is bigger.

items.p: Neha, a girl in Class 4 in Kochi, fills a measuring jug with 250 millilitres of water. She drops in a stone and the level rises to 310 millilitres. What is the volume of the stone, in millilitres?
items.why: 310 take away 250 is 60. The stone pushed aside 60 millilitres of water, so its volume is 60 millilitres.

items.p: Zoya says: 'Big things sink and small things float.' Give one example that shows she is wrong.
items.a: A big ship floats, and a small pebble sinks. So size alone does not settle it.
items.why: A strong answer gives an example that goes against the claim, such as a big thing that floats or a small thing that sinks, and says what that example shows.

items.p: Why is it easier to float in the sea than in a river?
opts: Salty water is denser than fresh water
The sea is warmer than a river
The sea has more waves
items.why: Salt dissolves in the water and makes it denser. A denser liquid pushes up harder, so things float higher in it.

items.p: Which one is the odd one out, and why? Wood, cork, ice, iron.
items.a: Iron, because it sinks. The other three float on water.
items.why: Wood, cork and ice are all less dense than water. Iron is almost 8 times denser than water.

items.p: A closed empty bottle floats because the air inside it weighs nothing at all.
items.why: False. Air does have weight, but a very small amount. The bottle floats because the air makes the whole bottle lighter than the water it pushes aside.

items.p: Draw a boat floating on water. Draw one arrow for the boat's weight and one for the upthrust. Make the arrows the right lengths.
items.a: A boat on the water, with a downward arrow for weight and an upward arrow for upthrust, both the same length.
items.why: A floating boat is balanced, so the arrows are equal. A strong drawing shows the arrows the same length, and the weight pointing down and the upthrust pointing up.

items.p: A thing floats when it is ____ dense than the liquid.
items.why: A thing that is less dense than the liquid is lighter than the same amount of the liquid, so it floats.

items.p: You push a plastic ball under water and then let go. It pops up to the surface. Why?
opts: The upthrust is bigger than the weight of the ball
The ball is angry
The water gets hotter
items.why: Under the water, the ball pushes aside a lot of water for its weight. The upthrust is bigger than the weight, and so it rises.

items.p: Ranjani, a girl in Class 4 in Chennai, says: 'A ship made of solid steel would float better than a hollow one, because steel is so strong.' Do you agree? Why?
items.a: No. A solid steel ship would be much denser than water and would sink. A hollow ship holds air and pushes aside much more water. Steel is strong, but it is the hollow shape that makes the ship float.
items.why: A strong answer separates strength from density, and says that a solid lump would push aside little water for its weight, while a hollow shape pushes aside a lot.

items.p: A potato sinks in tap water and floats in very salty water. What is the best explanation?
opts: The salt made the water denser than the potato
The salt made the potato lighter
The potato dried out
items.why: The potato was the same in both glasses. The salt dissolved and made the water denser. When the water is denser than the potato, the potato floats.

items.p: A small block has a volume of 10 millilitres and a mass of 8 grams. 10 millilitres of water has a mass of 10 grams. What will the block do in water?
opts: Float, because it is lighter than the same amount of water
Sink, because it is solid
Hover in the middle
items.why: The block has less mass than the same volume of water. That means it is less dense than water, so it floats.

items.p: Ice cubes float because ice is denser than water.
items.why: False. Ice floats because it is less dense than liquid water. When water freezes, it takes up about one tenth more space.

items.p: A floating boat pushes aside water that has the same ____ as the boat and its cargo.
items.why: This is Archimedes' principle. A floating thing pushes aside water that weighs as much as the thing itself.

items.p: Put these in the right order, for how a submarine dives and then comes back up.
a: Water flows into the ballast tanks
The submarine becomes heavier overall and sinks
Compressed air pushes the water out of the tanks
The submarine becomes lighter overall and rises
items.why: Taking in water makes the submarine denser, so it sinks. Pushing the water out makes it less dense, so it rises.

items.p: Pour each liquid gently into a glass of water. Does it float on the water, or sink to the bottom?
items.a: as given
items.why: Oils and petrol are less dense than water, so they float. Honey and syrups are full of sugar and are denser than water, so they sink.

items.p: A fish wants to rise towards the surface. What can she do?
opts: Put more gas into her swim bladder
Let all the gas out
Swallow a stone
items.why: More gas makes the fish less dense overall, so she floats upwards. Letting the gas out makes her denser, so she sinks.

items.p: A steel katori floats when it is set gently on the water. It sinks when it is pushed down and filled with water. Explain why, using the word air.
items.a: When the katori is empty, it holds a lot of air, so the katori and the air together are lighter than the water they push aside. When it fills with water, the air is gone, and the steel is denser than the water, so it sinks.
items.why: A strong answer says that the air pocket made the katori light for its size, and that filling it with water removed that advantage.

items.p: A ship sits lower in a river than in the sea. Why?
opts: River water is less dense than sea water, so the ship must push aside more of it
The river is warmer
The sea pulls the ship up
items.why: The ship must push aside water that weighs as much as the ship. Fresh water is less dense, so the ship sinks a little deeper to push aside enough.

items.p: Match each thing to the reason it floats or rises.
pairs: Helium balloon
helium is lighter than air
Hot air balloon
the heated air inside is less dense than the air around it
Banana-stem raft
the stems are full of air spaces
Coracle
a wide hollow basket holds air and pushes aside water
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each one is lighter for its size than the water or air around it. Air is held in the raft and the basket, and the gas or hot air is less dense in the balloons.

items.p: Selvi and Imran are both building foil boats. Each wants to carry as many coins as possible.

views.who: Selvi, a girl in Class 4 (an imagined view)
views.says: A wide, flat boat is best. It sits on a big area of water, and does not tip.

views.who: Imran, a boy in Class 4 (an imagined view)
views.says: A tall, deep boat is best. It holds more air, so it pushes aside more water.

items.ask: Whose view do you agree with more? What could you test to find out?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer picks a side, gives a reason, and describes a fair test, such as making both boats from the same size of foil and counting the coins each carries.
items.why: Both have a point. A wide boat is steady and a deep boat holds more air. The test is a fair test with the same foil and the same coins.

items.p: If two things both sink, the one with the bigger volume pushes aside more water.
items.why: True. When a thing is fully under the water, the water it pushes aside has the same volume as the thing itself. A bigger volume pushes aside more water.

items.p: Draw a glass with three layers: oil, water and syrup. Label which layer is on top and which is at the bottom, and write why.
items.a: A glass with oil on top, water in the middle and syrup at the bottom, with a short reason such as that oil is the least dense and syrup is the most dense.
items.why: A strong drawing puts the least dense liquid on top and the most dense at the bottom, and says that each liquid floats on a liquid that is denser than itself.

items.p: Which change would let a foil boat carry more cargo?
opts: A bigger hollow space that holds more air
A thicker layer of foil
Making the base rough
items.why: A bigger hollow space holds more air and pushes aside more water. More water pushed aside means more upthrust, and more cargo can be carried.

items.p: A boat pushes aside 120 cubic centimetres of water when it is just about to sink. One cubic centimetre of water has a mass of 1 gram. What is the most that the boat and its cargo can weigh, in grams?
items.why: The water pushed aside has a mass of 120 grams, so the upthrust is the weight of 120 grams. If the boat and cargo weigh more than that, it will sink.

items.p: The mark painted on the side of a ship that shows how deep it may sit in the water is called the ____ line.
items.why: A load line stops ships from being overloaded. It has different marks for sea water and fresh water.

items.p: Someone says: 'A potato sinks and a lemon floats, so potatoes are heavy and lemons are light.' What is missing from this sentence?
items.a: It leaves out the size. A big lemon can weigh more than a small potato. What matters is how heavy each one is for its size, which is its density.
items.why: A strong answer points out that weight alone does not settle it, and mentions size or density.

items.p: A potato sinks in tap water and floats in very salty water. You slowly pour plain water on top of the salty water. Describe what you think will happen to the potato and explain why.
items.a: The plain water floats on top of the salty water, because it is less dense. The potato floats in the salty layer, but it sinks through the plain water on top, and stops where the water is as dense as the potato, at the boundary between the two layers.
items.why: A strong answer says that the layers do not mix at first, that the plain layer is less dense, and that the potato sits where the liquid is dense enough to hold it up.

items.p: Ajay, a boy in Class 4 in Pune, has a boat that pushes aside 300 grams of water when the water reaches its rim. The boat weighs 40 grams. How many grams of cargo can it carry before it sinks?
items.why: The boat and cargo together can weigh as much as the water pushed aside, 300 grams. The boat itself weighs 40 grams, so the cargo can weigh 300 take away 40, which is 260 grams.

items.p: A block of wood floats with three quarters of itself under the water. What does this tell you about the wood?
opts: It is less dense than water, but not by a lot
It is much lighter than water
It is denser than water
items.why: Most of the block is under the water, so the wood is close to the density of water. A much lighter wood, such as balsa, would sit higher.

items.p: A ferry owner wants to carry more passengers than the load line allows.

views.says: I earn more with more passengers. The river is calm, and my ferry has crossed for years.
The load line is there for a reason. If waves come, a boat that sits too low can fill with water quickly.
I would like to travel cheaply, but I do not want to risk my life for a few extra rupees.

items.ask: Whose view do you agree with most? Why do you think rules like the load line exist?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer picks a side, gives a reason, and notes that a boat sitting low has less room before water comes in, so a small wave can sink it.
items.why: The load line is based on how a boat floats. The more a boat carries, the less spare room it has. Safety rules protect people on rough days.

items.p: Mala, a girl in Class 4 in Madurai, has two liquids, A and B, and one grape. She wants to find out which liquid is denser, without a scale. How could she do this?
items.a: Put the grape in each liquid. The liquid in which the grape floats higher is denser. If the grape floats in one and sinks in the other, the one where it floats is denser.
items.why: A strong answer uses the same thing in both liquids, and compares how high it floats. This is the idea of the hydrometer.

items.p: Match each clue to what it tells you.
pairs: A thing hovers in the middle of a liquid
its density is about the same as the liquid
A thing sinks to the bottom
it is denser than the liquid
A boat sits higher in the water than before
the liquid is denser, or the load is lighter
A thing floats on top
it is less dense than the liquid
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Where a thing sits in a liquid tells you how its density compares with the liquid. Hovering means about the same. Floating means less. Sinking means more.

items.p: A potato hovers in the middle of a glass of salty water. What is true?
opts: The potato and the salty water have almost the same density
The potato is much denser than the water
The potato is much lighter than the water
items.why: If the potato were denser, it would sink. If it were lighter, it would float. Hovering means that the potato and the water have almost the same density.

items.p: Ice floats because the water particles in ice are arranged in an open pattern that takes up more space.
items.why: True. When water freezes, its particles lock into an open pattern with gaps. The same amount of water takes up about one tenth more space as ice, so ice is less dense.

items.p: Every material that floats on water has a density less than ____ gram for each cubic centimetre.
items.why: Water has a density of 1 gram for each cubic centimetre. Anything with a smaller density floats on it.

items.p: Which one is the odd one out, and why? Ebony wood, iron, glass, cork.
items.a: Cork, because it floats. The other three are denser than water and sink.
items.why: Cork has a density of about a quarter of water. Ebony, iron and glass are all denser than water.

items.p: A cup with 10 coins floats in a basin of tap water. What happens to how high it sits when each of these changes happens?
items: the cup is moved to very salty water
the cup is moved from the sea to a river
the cup is moved from a river to the sea
items.a: as given
items.why: More load makes the cup sit lower. Denser water pushes up harder, so the cup sits higher. Less dense water makes it sit lower.

items.p: A coracle is round, wide and shallow. Why might that shape be good for crossing a shallow, rocky river?
items.a: A wide, shallow boat sits high in the water and does not go deep, so it does not hit rocks below. Its round shape also turns easily.
items.why: A strong answer says that a boat with a shallow draft needs little depth, and that a wide base is stable.

items.p: Draw a bottle diver in a bottle. Draw the air bubble in the diver before you squeeze and after you squeeze, and say what happens to the diver.
items.a: Two bottles, one with a larger air bubble and the diver near the top, and one with a smaller bubble and the diver sinking, with a note that squeezing squashes the air so the diver pushes aside less water.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the bubble getting smaller when squeezed and the diver sinking, with a reason about upthrust.

items.p: A hot air balloon rises. Which sentence is correct?
opts: The hot air inside is less dense than the cooler air outside
The hot air is heavier than the cooler air
The balloon is pulled up by the Sun
items.why: Heating makes air expand, so the same amount of air takes up more room and is less dense. The balloon rises in the denser, cooler air around it.

items.p: A swimming pool holds 100,000 litres of water. One litre of water has a mass of 1 kilogram. One tonne is 1,000 kilograms. How many tonnes of water is that?
items.why: 100,000 kilograms divided by 1,000 is 100 tonnes.

items.p: Whether a thing floats depends on both the thing and the liquid around it.
items.why: True. The same potato sinks in tap water and floats in salty water. The thing is the same, but the liquid is different.

quiz.p: What must be true for a solid thing to float in water?
opts: It is less dense than water
It is small
It is made of wood
quiz.why: A thing that is less dense than water is lighter than the same amount of water, so it floats. Size and material alone do not settle it.

quiz.p: A solid cube takes up the same space as 100 millilitres of water, but weighs 120 grams. 100 millilitres of water weighs 100 grams. What will the cube do?
opts: Sink
Float
Hover in the middle
quiz.why: The cube is heavier than the same amount of water, so it is denser, and it sinks.

quiz.p: What changes when you fold a foil ball into a foil boat?
opts: It pushes aside more water, because it holds a big space of air
The foil gets lighter
The foil becomes a different material
quiz.why: The foil is the same. The hollow shape holds air, and the shape pushes aside more water, so the upthrust is bigger.

quiz.p: A steel katori is set mouth up on water and floats. What inside the katori helps it float?
opts: Air
Steel
Sunlight
quiz.why: The air inside makes the katori and its air lighter than the water it pushes aside.

quiz.p: Maya, a girl in Class 4, wants a fair test of three boat shapes. Which thing must be the same for all three boats?
opts: The size of the foil, the water, and the way the coins are added
The shape of the boat
The number of coins each one carries
quiz.why: In a fair test, only one thing changes. Here the shape changes, so everything else, including the foil size and the loading, must stay the same.

quiz.p: One boat carries 12, 14 and 13 coins in three tries. What does this show?
opts: The result is steady, so we can trust it
The boat is broken
The test is not fair
quiz.why: Results that are close together show the test gives about the same answer each time, so we can trust it.

quiz.p: In which water is it easiest to float?
opts: Very salty water
Warm tap water
Cold fresh water
quiz.why: Salt makes water denser, and denser water pushes up harder. This is why people float easily in the Dead Sea.

quiz.p: A potato hovers in the middle of a glass of salty water. What does this mean?
opts: The potato and the water are about equally dense
The potato is much lighter than the water
The potato is much heavier than the water
quiz.why: A thing that is denser would sink. A thing that is less dense would float. Hovering means they have about the same density.

quiz.p: Why does ice float on water?
opts: Ice is less dense than liquid water
Ice is colder than water
Ice is smaller than water
quiz.why: When water freezes, it takes up more space. The same amount of water is less dense as ice, so ice floats.

quiz.p: You pour oil, water and honey slowly into a glass. Which layer is on top?
opts: The oil
The water
The honey
quiz.why: Oil is the least dense of the three, so it floats on top. Honey is the densest, so it sinks to the bottom.

quiz.p: How does a submarine rise to the surface?
opts: It pushes the water out of its ballast tanks with compressed air
It fills its tanks with more water
It switches off its engine
quiz.why: Pushing out the water makes the submarine lighter overall, so it is less dense and rises. Taking in water makes it sink.

quiz.p: Many people believe that heavy things sink. A steel ship floats. What does this show about the pattern?
opts: The pattern is not always true, so it must be tested
The ship is not really heavy
The pattern is always true
quiz.why: A pattern is something you notice, not a rule you can trust yet. One clear exception, such as a ship, shows that the pattern is incomplete and needs testing.

open_questions.q: Why is water so unusual that its solid form floats on its liquid form?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists understand the open pattern of ice. They are still arguing about why liquid water behaves in so many unusual ways.

open_questions.q: How did the first people discover that a hollow shape floats?
open_questions.why_open: No written records survive from that time. We only know that dugout canoes and reed rafts are very old.

open_questions.q: What is the best shape for a boat that must carry the most weight in rough water?
open_questions.why_open: The answer depends on the waves, the cargo and the material, and engineers are still improving designs.

open_questions.q: How do some insects, such as water striders, walk on water?
open_questions.why_open: They are held up by the skin of the water, called surface tension, which is a different idea from floating. Scientists are still finding out how their legs use it.

open_questions.q: Could a city on the sea float, and stay safe in storms?
open_questions.why_open: Some engineers are designing floating buildings and islands. They are still testing whether they can survive storms.

open_questions.q: Why do some deep-sea fish have no swim bladder?
open_questions.why_open: Gas is hard to hold under great pressure, and scientists are still working out how these fish stay at their depth.

maths.problem: A potato piece has a mass of 54 grams and a volume of 50 millilitres. 50 millilitres of water has a mass of 50 grams. Is the potato lighter or heavier than the same amount of water? By how many grams?
maths.explain: The potato is 54 grams and the same amount of water is 50 grams. 54 take away 50 is 4. The potato is heavier, so it is denser than water, and it sinks.
maths.why_maths: Comparing masses of the same volume is how you find out whether a thing is denser than water, without having to try it.

maths.problem: A foil boat has a base 13 centimetres by 13 centimetres, and the sides are 1 centimetre high. Its volume is 13 times 13 times 1 cubic centimetres. One cubic centimetre of water has a mass of 1 gram. A coin has a mass of about 4 grams. About how many coins can the boat carry before the water reaches the rim? Ignore the foil.
maths.explain: 13 times 13 is 169, so the volume is 169 cubic centimetres. The water pushed aside weighs 169 grams. 169 divided by 4 is about 42. In a real test you will carry fewer, because the boat tips.
maths.context: In the Foil Boats test, you fold foil into boats and count how many coins each can carry.
maths.why_maths: A calculation like this predicts the most a boat could carry, so you can compare your real result with the best possible one.

maths.problem: Look at the bar chart of the coins carried by three foil boats. How many more coins did boat B carry than boat C?
maths.explain: The bar for boat B is 41 and the bar for boat C is 17. 41 take away 17 is 24.
maths.context: In the Foil Boats test, boat A is wide and shallow, boat B is medium and boat C is narrow and deep. The chart shows made-up results.
maths.why_maths: A bar chart shows at a glance which boat carried the most, and the difference between two bars tells you how much better one design was.

maths.problem: In the Potato and the Salt test, a potato floated after 3 level tablespoons of salt in 250 millilitres of water. How many tablespoons of salt would you need for the same salty water in a 1 litre jug? One litre is 1,000 millilitres.
maths.explain: 1,000 millilitres is 4 times 250 millilitres. So you need 4 times as much salt. 4 times 3 is 12 tablespoons.
maths.context: In the Potato and the Salt test, you add salt to a glass of water one spoon at a time, until the potato floats.
maths.why_maths: Keeping the same ratio of salt to water gives you the same density of water, however much you make.

maths.problem: A big cargo ship carries 60,000 tonnes. One tonne is 1,000 kilograms. How many kilograms is that?
maths.explain: 60,000 times 1,000 is 60,000,000. That is sixty million kilograms.
maths.why_maths: Big numbers help us see how enormous a loaded ship is, and how much water it must push aside to float.

maths.problem: One litre of water has a mass of 1,000 grams. A one-rupee coin has a mass of about 4 grams. About how many one-rupee coins weigh the same as a litre of water?
maths.explain: 1,000 divided by 4 is 250. So about 250 coins weigh as much as a litre of water.
maths.why_maths: Comparing a litre of water to coins makes the idea of mass easier to picture, and shows how much a boat can really carry.

maths.problem: Sea water has about 35 grams of salt in every litre. The Dead Sea has about 340 grams of salt in every litre. About how many times saltier is the Dead Sea?
maths.explain: 340 divided by 35 is a little under 10, about 9.7. So the Dead Sea is about 10 times saltier.
maths.why_maths: Dividing the two amounts tells you how much saltier one water is than another, and explains why it holds people up so well.

maths.problem: About one tenth of a floating iceberg is above the water. An iceberg has a total volume of 10,000 cubic metres. How much of it is above the water?
maths.explain: One tenth of 10,000 is 10,000 divided by 10, which is 1,000. So 1,000 cubic metres is above the water, and 9,000 cubic metres is below.
maths.why_maths: Fractions show how much of an iceberg we can see, and why the part below the water is so much bigger. This is where the phrase tip of the iceberg comes from.

how_we_found_out.story: More than two thousand years ago, an ancient Greek thinker named Aristotle taught that broad, flat things float because of their shape, and that heavy things naturally go down. Around 250 BCE, in the Greek city of Syracuse, a mathematician named Archimedes tested this carefully. In his book On Floating Bodies, he showed that a liquid pushes up on anything in it, with a force equal to the weight of the liquid the thing pushes aside. Shape matters only because it changes how much liquid is pushed aside. A famous story says he found the idea in his bath and ran through the streets shouting 'Eureka!' Historians think that part is probably a legend, told two hundred years later by a Roman writer named Vitruvius. The book is real.
how_we_found_out.who: Archimedes of Syracuse, a Greek mathematician (about 287 to 212 BCE)
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Aristotle thought that shape alone decided whether a thing floated, and that heavy things simply belong down. Archimedes showed that a thing floats when the water it pushes aside weighs as much as the thing.
